# Performance

<!-- Generated by `python3 tests/hands-on/bench.py report` from docs/performance/results/. Don't edit this file: record a new run with bench.py, or change the text in tests/hands-on/tools/perf_report.py, then regenerate. -->

How fast the `umbraco` CLI is, how that is measured, and how to reproduce every number here. The CLI wraps
Umbraco's Management API, so most of a command's wall time is spent in Umbraco. The parts the CLI owns are
process startup, config and authentication, how many requests a command makes, and its own CPU: parsing,
writing output, and the export, diff and apply engines.

The [README](../README.md#performance) quotes CLI 0.1.0-alpha.15 on Umbraco 17.7.0 from the run of
[2026-09-29T10:12Z](performance/results/2026-09-29_101221_windows-amd-ryzen-9-7950x.json). Every run is under
[History across CLI versions](#history-across-cli-versions).

## Method

Three layers measure the CLI, each where it can measure reliably. Only the two deterministic ones can fail a
build.

| Layer | Measures | Runs | Can fail a build? |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Request counts](../tests/Umbraco.Cli.Tests/RequestCounts/) | HTTP requests per command, and token requests per run, against a fake Umbraco that records every request | `dotnet test`, on every pull request | Yes: exact counts |
| [BenchmarkDotNet](../tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks/README.md) | CPU time and allocated bytes of code the CLI owns, on in-memory fixtures | CI: pull requests labelled `performance`, weekly on `main`, on demand | Allocations: yes, more than 10% over `main`. Timings: no |
| [hyperfine](../tests/hands-on/README.md#benchmarks-benchpy) | End-to-end time, HTTP time and CLI overhead, per CLI build and Umbraco version | Locally, against the test harness's dev site | No: it reports |

### Request counts

The request-count tests
([`tests/Umbraco.Cli.Tests/RequestCounts/`](../tests/Umbraco.Cli.Tests/RequestCounts/)) run the shipped
command tree, client and authentication end to end, with only the transport replaced: a fake Umbraco answers
and records every request, the token exchange included. Each test pins how many requests a command makes, as a
formula over the fixture's size where the count depends on it (for example `ceil(n / 100)` tree pages for
`content tree` with n items at the root).

- **Catches:** a change that turns one request into one per item, a lost cache (a type read for every row, a
  token exchange for every request), and paging that asks for more pages than it needs. A failure names the
  command line, the expected and actual counts, the formula and every request sent.
- **Can't catch:** how long a request takes, the CLI's own CPU and allocations, or anything the real Umbraco
  does differently from the fake.

### BenchmarkDotNet allocation gate

[`tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks`](../tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks/README.md) measures startup wiring, the
output writers, Kiota response parsing, and the content and schema snapshot and diff engines, on deterministic
in-memory fixtures, so no Umbraco is involved. The [Benchmarks
workflow](https://github.com/worm-brain/Umbraco.Cli/actions/workflows/benchmarks.yml)
([`benchmarks.yml`](../.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml)) runs the pull request and `main` on the same runner
and fails when a benchmark's allocated bytes per operation rise more than 10% over `main`.

- **Catches:** an extra copy per item, a lost buffer reuse, or other new work per item that allocates, in code
  the CLI owns.
- **Can't catch:** network or server time, the number of requests, or (as a gate) CPU time: timings are in the
  job summary, but they don't fail the build.

Its results are not committed, so they are not on this page. Each run uploads its JSON reports as the
`benchmark-results` artifact (kept 90 days) of the [Benchmarks
workflow](https://github.com/worm-brain/Umbraco.Cli/actions/workflows/benchmarks.yml), and the job summary
shows the pull request against `main`.

### hyperfine end to end

[`tests/hands-on/bench.py`](../tests/hands-on/README.md#benchmarks-benchpy) times real commands with
[hyperfine](https://github.com/sharkdp/hyperfine) against the test harness's dev site: a local Umbraco with
the harness's fixture content, rebuilt for each Umbraco version so every run times the same content. Each CLI
build is installed side by side and run through its `umbraco` shim, as an installed tool runs. hyperfine gives
the end-to-end time (warm-up runs, then timed runs, with no shell and the output discarded). Separate
`--verbose` runs, which hyperfine never times, give the HTTP time: the CLI logs each response's duration, and
the HTTP time is the length of the union of those intervals, so concurrent requests count once. CLI overhead
is the end-to-end time minus the HTTP time. The results are committed to
[`docs/performance/results/`](performance/results/), and they are the only numbers on this page.

- **Catches:** what a user waits for, per CLI build and Umbraco version, and whether a change in that time is
  the CLI's (CLI overhead) or the server's (HTTP time).
- **Can't catch:** small regressions, reliably: it runs on one machine against a local site, and other load on
  the machine moves the numbers. It doesn't run in CI.

The scenarios (the `SCENARIOS` table in `bench.py`):

| Scenario | Command | What it exercises |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `umbraco --version` | startup only: no config, no HTTP |
| `get` | `umbraco content get <home>` | content get of the fixture home page |
| `list` | `umbraco data-type list --all` | a large list: every data type, each read by id |
| `content-export` | `umbraco content export --out <file>` | the whole fixture content tree to a file |
| `schema-diff` | `umbraco schema diff tests/hands-on/fixtures/schema.json` | the fixture schema snapshot against the site |

### Why timings never gate CI

- CI has no live Umbraco instance, by decision ([#139](https://github.com/worm-brain/Umbraco.Cli/issues/139),
  [#77](https://github.com/worm-brain/Umbraco.Cli/issues/77)), so end-to-end timing can't run there, and a run
  on one developer's machine can't gate anyone else's pull request.
- Timings on shared CI runners move between identical runs by more than the regressions worth catching. A
  threshold tight enough to catch one would fail at random; one loose enough not to would catch nothing.
- The likely regressions show up deterministically anyway: request fan-out as a higher request count, and
  extra work per item as more allocated bytes. So the gates are on counts and bytes, and timings are reported
  for people to read.

## Umbraco versions

Not yet measured. Every result so far is on Umbraco 17 (17.7.0). Once a run covers another major, this section
compares them. To measure it, run each version in one run on one machine:

```bash
python3 tests/hands-on/bench.py --cli local --umbraco 17,18
```

## Reproduce

Every command runs from the repository root. On Windows, type `python` for `python3`.

### Request counts

```bash
dotnet test tests/Umbraco.Cli.Tests --filter "FullyQualifiedName~RequestCount"
```

They need no Umbraco, and they also run in every `dotnet test`.

### BenchmarkDotNet

```bash
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks -- --filter "*" --job short
```

This is the job CI runs. To compare two builds the way the gate does:

```bash
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks -- --filter "*" --job short --artifacts ./bench/before
# ...make the change...
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks -- --filter "*" --job short --artifacts ./bench/after
pwsh ./scripts/ci/benchmark-compare.ps1 -Baseline ./bench/before -Candidate ./bench/after -BaselineLabel before -CandidateLabel after
```

See [its README](../tests/Umbraco.Cli.Benchmarks/README.md) for running one class or benchmark.

### The hyperfine runs on this page

These need the [test harness's requirements](../tests/hands-on/README.md#requirements) and hyperfine. Each
command repeats one committed run, and writes a new results file to compare with it. A published build that
isn't on nuget.org (a release that was packed but not pushed) installs from `./nupkg` or from `--source
<folder>`. Add `--note "<text>"` to record anything unusual about the run, such as other load on the machine.

[2026-09-29T10:12Z](performance/results/2026-09-29_101221_windows-amd-ryzen-9-7950x.json) on
windows-amd-ryzen-9-7950x. Its `local` build was commit 7d1a43a: run `git checkout 7d1a43a` first.

```bash
python3 tests/hands-on/bench.py --cli 0.1.0-alpha.6,0.1.0-alpha.15,local --umbraco 17.7.0 --warmup 3 --runs 10 --http-runs 5
```

### This page and the README section

```bash
python3 tests/hands-on/bench.py report
```

It reads every file in `docs/performance/results/`, rewrites this page, and rewrites only the block between
`<!-- perf:start -->` and `<!-- perf:end -->` in `README.md`. Running it again without new results changes
nothing. Commit a new results file and the regenerated pages together.

## Caveats

- **Noise.** Each number comes from one run on one machine. hyperfine's standard deviation is the spread to
  compare against: a difference smaller than the two results' spreads added together is noise. Other load on
  the machine (builds, test runs, other benchmarks) widens the spread and moves the means, so a run meant for
  committing should be on a quiet machine, and a run that wasn't says so in its note. Runs with a note:
  - [2026-09-29T10:12Z](performance/results/2026-09-29_101221_windows-amd-ryzen-9-7950x.json): Recorded on a
    busy machine (other workloads, including a BenchmarkDotNet run, ran alongside), so expect a wider spread
    than on a quiet machine.
- **End-to-end includes Umbraco.** It is what a user waits for: the CLI plus Umbraco's server time, here on a
  local site with the harness's small fixture content. A real site, a remote host or another Umbraco version
  moves it. Compare CLI overhead across CLI builds, and HTTP time across Umbraco versions.
- **HTTP time is more than server time.** It is everything inside the HTTP stack. In particular, the first
  request of each process opens the connection (TCP and the TLS handshake) and pays for the first use of
  .NET's HTTP stack, so a command that makes any request has some HTTP time even when Umbraco answers at once.
- **CLI overhead includes reading response bodies.** The CLI's clock for a request stops at the response
  headers, so reading the body counts as CLI overhead. On localhost that part is small.
- **Only requests a build logs are counted.** Builds before 0.1.0-alpha.15 don't log the OAuth token exchange
  under `--verbose`, and builds before 0.1.0-alpha.14 have no token cache, so they exchange a token on every
  run. For those builds (such as 0.1.0-alpha.6) the token round trip is in CLI overhead, and it is missing
  from their request counts.
- **Logged durations are whole milliseconds,** truncated, so bench.py adds half a millisecond to each.
- **Builds do different work.** A later build's command can make more requests than an earlier one's (more
  follow-up reads, for a fuller result), so compare the request counts before the times. A failed row is a
  build without that command or snapshot format, not a slow one.
- **Machines differ.** Numbers from different machines aren't comparable. Compare rows from the same machine.
